history.action: route plan -> implement -> review -> qa (model, confidence 88)

validated_work_order.understanding: A category filter value like `%%%%%%Z` typed into a Custom report freezes the browser's main thread for minutes on a budget with several hundred categories. The path is synchronous and inside React's render: CustomReport.tsx marks a `category` + `contains/doesNotContain/matches/hasTags` condition as `isComplexCategoryCondition`, which routes the report through `createCustomSpreadsheet` and `createGroupedSpreadsheet`, whose bodies call `narrowCategoriesByConditions` -> `filterCategoriesByConditions` -> `likePatternToRegex('%' + value + '%')` once per category per condition, every render. Each unescaped `%` compiles to `.*`, so six `%` is an 8-wildcard pattern, and `.test()` backtracks over the partitions of the category name. The cost is in `.test()`, not in compilation - I measured compilation at <=0.04 ms in every row of the table - so memoisation cannot be the fix. `unicodeLike` (the sqlite `UNICODE_LIKE` scalar) goes through the same function and already memoises through an LRU, so it needs neither a second bound nor its own cache. The bound belongs in `likePatternToRegex` and must be expressible in its return type, because a caller that cannot see a refusal will silently compile the catastrophic regex. It must fail OPEN: a refusal keeps every category, on both operators - including `doesNotContain`, which is the trap, because a refusal represented as a match-everything regex negates to 'drop everything' and drops every category the query fetched. The ticket's three cleanup findings were each verified to have zero external consumers.
validated_work_order.root_cause: Unbounded wildcard expansion in the LIKE-pattern compiler. `likePatternToRegex` (packages/loot-core/src/shared/likePattern.ts:16) translates every unescaped `%` into `.*` with no limit, and the regex engine backtracks roughly 7x per additional wildcard over the partitions of the subject string on `.test()`. The report axis runs that `.test()` once per category per condition on every render, so a value with six `%` is an 8-wildcard pattern against every category name. The cost is in matching, not compiling: compilation stayed at <=0.04 ms for every pattern I measured, so caching the regex (which `unicodeLike` already does) cannot fix it.
validated_work_order.approach:
Make `likePatternToRegex` return `RegExp | null`, refusing a pattern that is over-long or over-wildcarded, and teach its two consumers to treat `null` as 'matches every string' so the failure direction is open everywhere.

1. The bound, in `likePattern.ts` only: two module-private constants - `MAX_PATTERN_LENGTH = 256` (the same number and precedent as the `matches` guard at budgetDataQuery.ts:274-278) and `MAX_UNESCAPED_WILDCARDS = 4`. Count only unescaped `%` and `?`; a `\\%` compiles to a literal and adds no `.*`. Return `null` before `new RegExp(...)` is ever constructed. The wildcard count, not the length, is what carries AC-1: six `%` is an 8-character pattern no length cap would catch.

2. Why 4, measured on this runner (300 categories, ~40-char names, value = `%`x n + 'Z'): 3 wildcards 7.5 ms, 4 → 85 ms, 5 → 868 ms, 6 → 6.5 s, 7 → 49.2 s, 8 → >120 s (stopped). Compile ≤0.04 ms in every row, ~7x per added wildcard - the shape of the epic's figures. A cap of 4 keeps the accepted region at ≤85 ms across 300 categories and cuts everything from 868 ms upward. It also preserves the pinned behaviour: `contains '%'` and `contains '?'` compile to 3-wildcard patterns and still match everything.

3. Why `RegExp | null` and not a match-everything regex. THE TRAP: `contains` keeps a category when the regex matches, `doesNotContain` keeps it when it does NOT. Returning `/^[\s\S]*$/i` therefore fails OPEN for `contains` and fails CLOSED for `doesNotContain` - it drops every category, the money-losing direction AC-3 exists to prevent. `null` forces each call site to decide explicitly and TypeScript refuses to let a future consumer forget.

THE RULE: a refused pattern is treated as matching every string, and every consumer of a refusal KEEPS every category - including the `doesNotContain` branch, which returns `true` on a refusal rather than negating a match-everything result.

WORKED EXAMPLES (computed, value `%%%%%%Z`, 8 wildcards, refused): `contains` → axis keeps all N categories; query `$like` → `UNICODE_LIKE` returns 1 for every row → every transaction returned; axis == result set, totals unchanged, real balances. `doesNotContain` → axis keeps all N categories (NOT zero); query `$notlike` → `NOT 1` → no transactions; axis strictly WIDER than the result set, every kept category at 0.00.

INVARIANT: for any refused pattern and any budget, the categories the axis renders are a SUPERSET of those in the query's result set - no category the query fetched loses its row, no money leaves a total because a value was too long. Every refusal path returns 'keep', so the bound cannot violate it.

HOW THAT LOOKS ON SCREEN (the correction to the last plan): a `doesNotContain` filter holding a refused value gives every category a balance of 0.00, so the screen depends on `showEmpty`, which defaults to false (ReportOptions.ts:25). With showEmpty false, `filterEmptyRows` (filterEmptyRows.ts:24) drops every zero-balance row and the report renders an empty table - identical for a correct and a fail-closed build, so it is not a usable assertion. With showEmpty true, every category survives at 0.00; a fail-closed build narrows the axis to nothing and grouped-spreadsheet.ts:50 takes `categoryList.length === 0` and calls `setData([])`. AC-3 therefore runs with 'Show empty rows' enabled.

4. `unicodeLike` treats a refusal as a match and returns 1, keeping the invariant on the query side too. One mechanical consequence: the cache's `if (!cachedRegExp)` must become an `=== undefined` sentinel, since a cached `null` is falsy and would recompile per row.

5. The three cleanups ride along: unexport `REGEX_SPECIAL`, unexport `canNarrowAxisByConditions` with the reason recorded next to it, delete the `// ? added here` scar.

files.change: Add two module-private constants - `MAX_PATTERN_LENGTH = 256` and `MAX_UNESCAPED_WILDCARDS = 4`, both unexported - and change the signature to `export function likePatternToRegex(pattern: string): RegExp | null`. Return `null` when `pattern.length > MAX_PATTERN_LENGTH` before compiling anything. Inside the existing while loop keep a `wildcards` counter incremented only on the unescaped `%` and unescaped `?` branches - NOT on the escaped-wildcard branch, where `\\%` compiles to a literal - and return `null` when the count exceeds `MAX_UNESCAPED_WILDCARDS`, before `new RegExp(regexStr, 'i')` is ever constructed. Extend the module doc comment with the contract every consumer now depends on: 'returns null for a pattern it refuses; a refused pattern is to be treated as matching every string, and the caller must then keep everything rather than drop it'. Add the measured table (3/4/5/6/7 wildcards -> 7.5 ms / 85 ms / 868 ms / 6.5 s / 49.2 s across 300 categories, compile <=0.04 ms throughout) and say in one line why the bound is the fix and not memoisation. Delete the trailing `// ? added here`; keep `// escaped wildcard - treat as literal character` above it. Drop `export` from `REGEX_SPECIAL` (line 14), keeping both in-module uses on lines 25 and 35.
files.why: The file the ticket says the bound is defined in, and the only place both consumers inherit it. The `null` return makes a refusal visible to a caller instead of silently compiling the catastrophic regex.

files.change: Retype the LRU to `new LRUCache<string, RegExp | null>({ max: 500 })`. Replace `if (!cachedRegExp)` with an `=== undefined` sentinel (`let cached = likePatternCache.get(pattern); if (cached === undefined) { cached = likePatternToRegex(pattern); likePatternCache.set(pattern, cached); }`) - a cached `null` is falsy, so the existing check would recompile per row instead of caching the refusal. After the lookup, `if (cached === null) return 1;` with a comment stating why a refusal returns a MATCH: under `$like` that returns every transaction (equal to the axis, which also keeps everything) and under `$notlike` none (a strict subset of the axis), so in both directions the axis is never narrower than the result set. Add no second bound and no second memoisation.
files.why: AC-2 requires the sqlite UNICODE_LIKE path to inherit the bound rather than grow a second check, so this consumer handles `null` and nothing more.

files.change: Three edits. (1) `contains` branch (~line 246): hoist `const pattern = getNormalisedString('%' + condition.value + '%')` and `const matcher = likePatternToRegex(pattern)`, guard `if (typeof condition.value !== 'string') return false;` to preserve today's exact semantics, and return `matcher === null || matcher.test(getNormalisedString(textValue))`. (2) `doesNotContain` branch (~line 258): the same hoist, and return `matcher === null ? true : !matcher.test(getNormalisedString(textValue))` - a refusal must return `true` and KEEP the category, with a comment naming the trap: negating a match-everything result would drop every category, the money-losing direction. Keep the existing comments on why the axis runs the query's two primitives; `isSupportedCategoryCondition` already guarantees a string value, so the new guards are defensive only. (3) Drop `export` from `canNarrowAxisByConditions` (line 89; sole caller line 137 of the same file, imported by no test) and record in its doc comment that it is unexported rather than given a direct test because all four branches are already covered through its only observable contract, `narrowCategoriesByConditions`'s - budgetDataQuery.test.ts lines 403/416, 436, 452 and 350. `matches` at lines 274-284 is untouched.
files.why: The axis is the money path. Both LIKE call sites must decide the refusal explicitly, and `doesNotContain` is the one that decides it the wrong way by default.

files.change: Create with YAML frontmatter `category: Bugfixes` and `authors: [Shivam-Fl]`, then a body of exactly one line and no trailing newline in it, e.g.: 'Stop Custom reports freezing when a category filter value is packed with wildcard characters such as `%%%%%%`.' cases: Add a module-level helper `matches(pattern, value)` that calls `likePatternToRegex`, throws if it returns null, and returns `.test(value)` - then route the ~15 existing assertions through it. Required by the type change, and it doubles as the AC-4 regression suite: every existing case (`%%%` matching every string, `\\%` as a literal, `_` NOT a wildcard, case-insensitivity) now also proves the bound refuses nothing plausible. No non-null assertion.

New describe block 'bounds the pattern': `likePatternToRegex('%'.repeat(6) + 'Z')` is null (8 unescaped wildcards) and `likePatternToRegex('%'.repeat(5))` is null - the exact 8-wildcard value AC-1 names.
Boundary from both sides: a 4-wildcard pattern such as `'%' + '%%Z' + '%'` is NOT null and still matches, so the cap is 4 and not 3.
The count is over UNESCAPED wildcards only: `'\\%'.repeat(20)` is not refused, because it compiles to literals and adds no `.*`.
Length cap independently: `'x'.repeat(257)` is null, `'x'.repeat(256)` is not, matching the existing 256-character guard at budgetDataQuery.ts:274-278.
A refused pattern is refused structurally rather than by cost - the return is null, not a RegExp. Do NOT write a wall-clock timing assertion; it would be flaky in CI.
Falsifiability, required by .sdlc/memory/conventions.md: raise `MAX_UNESCAPED_WILDCARDS` to 99 in a scratch edit, record the failing run showing 'bounds the pattern' going green-to-red, revert.

`unicodeLike('%%%%%%Z', 'Food')` returns 1 - a refused pattern is a match on the query side, keeping the axis from being narrower than the result set under `$like`. Under `$notlike` the compiler emits `(NOT UNICODE_LIKE(...) OR left IS NULL)`, so the same value yields no transactions, a strict subset of the axis.

The refusal is cached rather than recompiled: call `unicodeLike` twice with the same refused pattern and assert the LRU holds it. RUN THIS FILE WITH `yarn workspace @actual-app/core run test:node -- src/platform/server/sqlite/unicodeLike.test.ts`. It is collected by the NODE config, not the web one: `packages/loot-core/vitest.config.ts` excludes only `src/platform/server/sqlite/index.test.ts` and `src/platform/server/fs/index.test.ts` and otherwise uses the default `**/*.test.ts` include, whereas `vitest.web.config.ts` sets `include:` to exactly those two files, so a CLI path argument against the web config matches nothing and runs zero tests. `package.json` `test` -> `npm-run-all -cp 'test:*'` -> `test:node`, so CI runs this file today. Do NOT pass `-t`: that hazard belongs to the two files that share process state via the sql.js wasm fetch, not to this file.
Pre-existing behaviour the cap must not change: `unicodeLike('%%%', 'Food')` and `unicodeLike('%?%', 'Food')` still return 1 - both 3-wildcard patterns, under the cap.
`unicodeLike(null, 'Food')` and `unicodeLike('', 'Food')` still return 0, so the early return is untouched by the retype.

In the 'reads text operators as LIKE patterns' describe, the AC-3 case for `contains`: `filterBy('contains', '%%%%%%Z')` equals `allIds` (all five wildcardCategories) - a refused pattern keeps every category rather than narrowing.

The paired `doesNotContain` case: `filterBy('doesNotContain', '%%%%%%Z')` ALSO equals `allIds`. The fail-closed trap and the single most important assertion in the change - if the axis empties here, money has left every total. Add a comment saying so. This unit assertion, not the browser step, carries IAC-3 directly.

The boundary case in the other direction: `filterBy('contains', '%%Z')` (4 wildcards, accepted) narrows exactly as the pattern says rather than keeping everything, so a fix that made every text condition a no-op fails here.

The grouped axis too, through `narrowCategoriesByConditions` rather than the helper: a `contains '%%%%%%Z'` condition returns the input BY IDENTITY (`toBe(axis)`), the existing contract for 'did not narrow', which is what stops the grouped array being rebuilt and empty groups deleted. Assert the same identity for `doesNotContain '%%%%%%Z'`.

Re-run the existing pinned cases unchanged and say so in the commit body: `contains '%'` and `contains '?'` keep every category, `contains '\\%'` narrows to `['c-discount']`, `contains 'o%'` narrows to three, `doesNotContain '%'` is `[]`, `matches 'x'.repeat(257)` keeps every category.
Falsifiability: invert the `doesNotContain` refusal to `matcher === null ? false : ...`, record the failing run, revert.

qa_script: Boot with `yarn start`, choose "Don't use a server", then click "Try the demo" (WelcomeScreen.tsx:130 - the button reads 'Try the demo', not 'View demo') for a populated budget. Note its size: 7 categories (Food, General, Bills, Bills (Flexible), Income, Starting Balances, Savings), far short of the several hundred IAC-1 names - see step 12.

Open Reports -> Custom report. Set the graph to 'Data Table' (ReportTopbar.tsx:96) so rows are readable. Open the sidebar and turn ON 'Show empty rows' (Options -> 'Show empty rows', ReportSidebar.tsx:494). It is OFF by default and every money assertion below depends on it being on. Note the full unfiltered category list - that is the reference set.

Add a filter: topbar Filters button -> field Category -> operator contains -> value `%%%%%%Z`. Assert the table renders promptly and the category list still shows every category from the reference set, with its real balance.
While that value is in place, keep typing and deleting characters in the filter field: the page stays responsive. This is the browser-observable form of 'the main thread was not blocked'.

Switch the operator to doesNotContain with the same value `%%%%%%Z`. Assert the category list is STILL the complete reference set, every row reading 0.00. THIS IS THE MONEY ASSERTION: with 'Show empty rows' on, an empty table here means the axis was dropped rather than kept and every category the query would have fetched has lost its row. (With it off, this same configuration legitimately renders empty, because the query returns nothing and filterEmptyRows.ts:24 drops zero-balance rows - so an empty report under the default setting is expected, not a defect. Turn the toggle on before concluding anything.)

Set the sidebar 'Split:' select to 'Category'. There is no separate Grouped report page - ReportRouter.tsx routes only to Custom reports; the grouped surface is this same Custom report, whose rows then come from `data.groupedData` built by `createGroupedSpreadsheet`. Assert every group survives and each still contains all of its categories rather than only the matching ones. Repeat steps 3 and 5 under this split.

Positive control at the cap boundary: with operator contains, value `%%Z` narrows the axis the way the pattern says (4 wildcards, accepted); value `%%%Z` is refused and keeps every category. Assert the two behave differently - a fix that made every text condition a no-op fails here.

Negative controls, unchanged from today: `Food` narrows to the food categories; `oo` narrows to Food only; `%` keeps every category; `?` keeps every category; `\%` narrows to the one category whose name contains a literal percent sign; `_` does NOT act as a wildcard.
Length bound: a 40-character ordinary substring narrows normally; a 300-character run of `x` keeps every category.
Reload the page, confirm the filter survived (the report restores from sessionStorage) and that the axis is still complete with 'Show empty rows' still on.

Collect console and pageerror for the whole run and assert nothing uncaught was emitted. Per .sdlc/memory/qa/environment.md both channels arrive out of band, so read them after an unconditional settle wait, and expect ordinary dev-mode noise rather than demanding silence.

Record what the demo budget could and could not show: with 7 categories an 8-wildcard pattern costs about 5 ms in total (measured), so the pre-fix multi-minute hang is not reproducible there and no stopwatch result from this run should be read as evidence either way for AC-1's timing - that evidence is AC-8's structural guarantee. If QA can reach a budget with several hundred categories, time the render with and without the refused value and put both numbers in the report.
risks: The fail-closed trap in `doesNotContain` is the one mistake this change can make, and it is silent: a refusal implemented as a match-everything regex narrows `contains` correctly while dropping every category under `doesNotContain`, so the axis becomes narrower than the query's result set and categories the query fetched lose their money from every total - the defect class PR #9 fixed. Called out in files[], tests[], AC-3, AC-9 and the QA script.

The browser cannot distinguish a correct build from the fail-closed bug unless 'Show empty rows' is on: under `doesNotContain` a refused value gives the query no transactions, and with the default showEmpty=false every row is then dropped as zero. QA turning the toggle on is a step in qa_script and both AC-3 and its how_to_verify say so explicitly. If it is missed, a correct build reads as broken - the same failure mode the last review caught, now named rather than assumed.

Widening the return type to `RegExp | null` is a breaking change to a shared module. Both existing consumers are updated here and TypeScript prevents a silent third, but a consumer added outside this repo would need to handle the refusal.

The `if (!cachedRegExp)` sentinel in `unicodeLike` must change to `=== undefined` in the same diff, or a cached `null` recompiles the pattern on every row - a performance regression rather than a correctness one, and the kind that survives review because the tests still pass.

The cap of 4 was measured against ~40-character category names. A pathologically long name would raise the accepted region's cost, since backtracking scales with subject length. Names are user input and bounded in practice, and this is strictly better than the unbounded behaviour it replaces.

The measurements were taken with Node's V8 regex engine on this runner; the browser ships the same engine, but absolute milliseconds will differ from a user's machine. The shape - roughly 7x per additional wildcard - is what the cap relies on, and it held across every row.

AC-2 hands QA a command that actually collects the file (`test:node`) rather than one that silently runs zero files; the previous plan's web-config command collected nothing because `vitest.web.config.ts` whitelists exactly two files. If a future change moves unicodeLike.test.ts into either of those paths this command's scope changes with it, and the how_to_verify text names both config files so the next reader can check.

No file in `forbidden_paths` is touched: three source files in `packages/` plus one new file under `upcoming-release-notes/`. No new host is contacted - the app's existing reads of api.github.com and raw.githubusercontent.com are unchanged and both are already in `env.api_allowlist`.
out_of_scope: Bounding the query-side per-transaction `matches` / `$regexp` regex in `packages/loot-core/src/server/aql/compiler.ts`, which the epic notes is already slow and is larger there. The axis's 256-character guard at budgetDataQuery.ts:274-278 is left exactly as it is; the length cap here copies that precedent rather than replacing it.
Routing the Sankey and Budget Analysis reports through the shared pattern - the text-operator piece, a separate ticket.

Any memoisation added to `likePatternToRegex` or to the report axis. `unicodeLike` already holds an LRU and compilation measures at <=0.04 ms, so caching cannot be the fix and no cache is added or removed.

Lowering the cap, exporting either constant, or making the bound configurable per report. The numbers are stated in the module and the measurement recorded beside them; tuning them later is its own change.
Changing `matches` behaviour on the axis in any way, including routing it through the new bound. It is not a LIKE pattern and its divergence from the query is already axis-wider.

Getting the browser's main thread off this work altogether - moving the axis narrowing off the render path, memoising the narrowed axis, web-workerising it. This change makes the pathological input cheap; it does not restructure the synchronous render.

alternatives_considered.approach: Return a match-everything RegExp (`/^[\s\S]*$/i`) for a refused pattern instead of `null`, leaving both call sites untouched.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It fails OPEN for `contains` and fails CLOSED for `doesNotContain`: that branch keeps a category when the regex does NOT match, so negating 'matches everything' drops every category - the axis becomes narrower than the query's result set and every category the query fetched loses its money from every total. The exact defect AC-3 exists to prevent, and it would have passed a `contains`-only test.

alternatives_considered.approach: Keep AC-3's browser assertion with 'Show empty rows' at its default (off), on the reasoning that an empty doesNotContain report is the tell.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It is not a tell. With showEmpty false, `filterEmptyRows` (filterEmptyRows.ts:24) drops every zero-balance row, so the query's empty result set renders an empty table on a correct implementation too - the two are the same picture. The only browser setting that separates them is showEmpty true, where correct shows the full axis at 0.00 and fail-closed shows nothing. This is what the last review objected to and it is right.

alternatives_considered.approach: Keep `likePatternToRegex` total and add a sibling `isPatternWithinBounds(pattern)` that consumers must remember to call.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It leaves the unbounded compile reachable - a caller that forgets the check gets the catastrophic regex with nothing to stop it, which is the hazard the ticket names when it says the bound must live inside the function. It also splits one definition of the pattern language across two exports in the file that declares itself the single definition.

alternatives_considered.approach: Throw from `likePatternToRegex` on a refused pattern and let each caller catch.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: `unicodeLike` is a sqlite scalar function invoked per row from inside the query engine; an exception there escapes as a raw engine error rather than a fail-open result, and a per-row try/catch is the wrong shape for a control-flow signal on the hottest path in the file.

alternatives_considered.approach: Bound the value at the report UI - strip or reject wildcard characters in the Category filter field.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It fixes one entry point and leaves every other one unbounded: transaction rules reach the same `$like` path through `transaction-rules.ts:659`, and so does `forecast-filters.ts:241`. It also cannot satisfy AC-2, which requires the bound to live in the shared function.

alternatives_considered.approach: Fix the hang by memoising `likePatternToRegex` in the report axis.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: The epic's measurement is right and I confirmed it on this runner: compilation was <=0.04 ms for every pattern, including the 7-wildcard one that takes 49.2 s to test. Caching the regex would remove a fraction of a percent of the cost. The bound is the fix.

alternatives_considered.approach: Give `canNarrowAxisByConditions` a direct test instead of unexporting it (the other branch AC-6 allows).
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: All four branches are already covered through `narrowCategoriesByConditions`, its only caller and only observable contract (budgetDataQuery.test.ts lines 403/416, 436, 452, 350). A second table asserting the same four outcomes through a private function is exactly the kind of test that drifts from the first, and it would keep a gate with no independent meaning exported for a future caller to depend on. The reason is recorded next to the function, as AC-6 requires.

alternatives_considered.approach: Carry AC-3 entirely as a unit assertion (narrowCategoriesByConditions returning the input `toBe(axis)`) and drop its browser half.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: Allowed by the last review, but it leaves the ticket's second surface - what a person sees in the report - unverified in the product, and the unit test cannot reach `filterEmptyRows`, the one place where a correct axis is turned back into an empty screen. The two halves together make the fail-closed direction non-vacuous, so the browser half is kept - with the toggle on.

assumptions: The wildcard count, not the pattern length, is what bounds the cost. Confirmed by measurement: a 6-character value producing an 8-wildcard pattern is where AC-1's hang lives, and no length cap below ~6 would touch it.

4 is the right cap. It keeps the accepted region at <=85 ms across 300 categories (measured), admits every value the existing pinned tests exercise (`%` and `?` compile to 3-wildcard patterns), and admits any realistic user input - no plausible category filter contains three or more unescaped wildcards.

Treating a refusal as a match on the query side (`unicodeLike` -> 1) is the correct pairing with an axis that keeps every category, because it makes the query's result set a subset of the axis in both operator directions. The alternative pairing (refusal -> 0) also satisfies the subset invariant, so the choice is made on least surprise: `contains` returns everything and `doesNotContain` returns nothing, rather than the reverse.
`isSupportedCategoryCondition` already guarantees `typeof condition.value === 'string'` for `contains` and `doesNotContain`, so the new non-string guards are defensive and do not change behaviour.

The report axis runs synchronously in the React component body (custom-spreadsheet.ts:93, grouped-spreadsheet.ts:45), which is why the freeze is on the main thread and why the bound is worth having on this path even though the query-side UNICODE_LIKE runs elsewhere.

QA can reach 'Show empty rows' in the Custom report's sidebar Options popover in the running app. The control is wired at ReportSidebar.tsx:494 (`name: 'show-empty-items'`, text 'Show empty rows') and its handler sets `showEmpty` on both the session report and the passed setter; if it is disabled for some configuration QA uses, AC-3's unit assertion still carries IAC-3 directly.
unknowns: How much of AC-1 a QA run can actually observe. The demo budget has 7 categories and I measured an 8-wildcard pattern against those 7 names at 5.4 ms in total, so the pre-fix multi-minute hang is not reproducible there. AC-1 is written to what a live browser can see and AC-8 carries the falsifiable form of the same claim; if QA can reach a budget with several hundred categories, the timing is worth measuring and recording in the PR.

Whether any consumer outside this repository imports `REGEX_SPECIAL`. The package's `exports` map exposes `./shared/*` as a direct file path, so the name was reachable; a repo-wide grep across packages/, scripts/, docs/ and upcoming-release-notes/ found no reference outside its own module, and this package is not published for third-party consumption as `@actual-app/core` in any configuration I could see.
validated_work_order.debate_summary: Two objections were raised against version 1 of this plan and both are answered from the code rather than from recollection. Objection 1: AC-3's browser half and qa_script steps 5 and 6 asserted that a doesNotContain filter holding `%%%%%%Z` still shows the complete category list at default report settings, where an empty result set renders as an empty table - so the assertion failed on a correct implementation and could not distinguish it from the fail-closed bug it exists to catch. Agreed, and the acceptance criteria, the qa_script and risks[] now agree with each other: AC-3 runs with 'Show empty rows' ENABLED (sidebar Options -> 'Show empty rows', ReportSidebar.tsx:494), qa_script turns it on as its own step (step 2) before the doesNotContain assertion, AC-3 and AC-9 state plainly that under the default setting an empty doesNotContain report is the expected outcome of a correct build, and the old 'if it empties here, the bound is failing closed' note is reworded: an empty table with the toggle ON is the failure signal, an empty table with it OFF is not. The unit assertion remains and is named as the direct carrier of IAC-3 ('asserted directly ... by showing the axis still carries the full category set'), with the browser half proving the kept axis survives `filterEmptyRows` - the one place a correct axis becomes an empty screen. Objection 2: AC-2's how_to_verify and the tests[] entry for unicodeLike.test.ts handed over `vitest --run -c vitest.web.config.ts <file>`, which collects zero files, because `vitest.web.config.ts` sets `include:` to exactly `platform/server/sqlite/index.test.ts` and `platform/server/fs/index.test.ts` and a CLI path argument only filters what `include` discovers. Confirmed from the config files rather than from the memory entry, and corrected to `yarn workspace @actual-app/core run test:node -- src/platform/server/sqlite/unicodeLike.test.ts` in both places, with the reason written down (`vitest.config.ts` excludes only those two paths and otherwise uses the default `**/*.test.ts` include, so `test:node` collects the file and CI already runs it via `test` -> `npm-run-all -cp 'test:*'`). The adjacent 'Do NOT pass -t' instruction is dropped: that hazard belongs to the two files that share process state through the sql.js wasm fetch, not to unicodeLike.test.ts. Two further corrections came out of walking the UI path: the demo button is labelled 'Try the demo' (WelcomeScreen.tsx:130), not 'View demo', and there is no separate Grouped report page - ReportRouter.tsx routes only to Custom reports, and the grouped surface is the same Custom report with 'Split:' set to Category, whose rows come from `data.groupedData`. Nothing else from the rejection changed the design: the bound still lives in `likePatternToRegex` and still returns `null`, still fails open on both operators, and the cap is still 4.
residual_risks: If a future report grows a third LIKE consumer, the type change forces it to handle the refusal, but nothing forces it to handle it in the OPEN direction. The invariant is written into the module doc comment and asserted on both operators, so the next review has something to check against.

AC-3's browser half depends on QA performing the 'Show empty rows' step. The toggle is now step 2 of the qa_script and named in the criterion's how_to_verify, but a QA run that skips it will see an empty doesNotContain report on a correct build. That is why the paired unit assertion (`filterBy('doesNotContain', '%%%%%%Z')` equals `allIds`) is required rather than optional: IAC-3 is carried by the test even if the browser half is skipped.
